leads.story: Slovakia's register of protected trees files this lime under an address that is not where protected trees usually end up: the courtyard of a former creche, in the middle of the Váh housing estate in Šaľa. The state's reason for protecting it is set out in the register in plain words. It stands out for its mighty growth and its health, and it is valued for the local microclimate, for its seed and for how it looks. What the register does not carry is a number. No girth, no height, no age, which is true of most entries on that list. Figures for this tree circulate online and none of them traces back to a page solid enough to print, so this page stays empty rather than confident. Slovak Wikipedia's national list of protected trees carries the same entry, S 163, and confirms the species as Tilia cordata. Small-leaved lime is the tree of central European squares and courtyards, planted for shade and for the flowers, which open in the second half of June and make the whole crown audible with bees for a fortnight. One thing to know before you go: a creche courtyard is not a park. It may be fenced, and no source settles whether you can walk in or only look from the pavement. Anyone in Šaľa could settle it in one message.
leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, small hearts with rusty tufts in the vein angles beneath. It stands in the courtyard of the former creche on the Váh estate, protected for its size, so look for the biggest crown there.
